12546.title: Feature Transformation
12546.heading: Feature Transformation
12546.content:
Feature transformation constructs new variables from existing variables through a mathematical or statistical mapping. A logarithm, ratio, square, standardization, projection, or composition of several functions can expose relationships that are difficult for a learner to use in the original representation.

A transformation preserves a connection to the input features, unlike some forms of domain-specific feature generation. Its value is judged by the downstream analytic task, not by novelty alone.

12548.title: Feature Transformation Recommendation

12549.sourceSearchName: feature transformation recommendation feature transformation recommendation
12549.title: Feature Transformation Recommendation
12549.heading: Feature Transformation Recommendation
12549.content:
Feature transformation recommendation predicts which operation is likely to improve a given variable or dataset. A recommender can learn from earlier transformation outcomes rather than testing every function.

Compact distribution summaries, including quantile-based sketches, provide inputs to recommendation models. The system's generality depends on the diversity of prior datasets and on respecting feature types and operation requirements.

12552.sourceSearchName: feature transformation graph feature transformation graph
12552.title: Feature Transformation Graph
12552.heading: Feature Transformation Graph
12552.content:
A feature transformation graph represents datasets as nodes and transformation operations as directed edges. A child node contains features produced from its parent, while combination nodes can unite features from several paths.

The graph records derivation history and exposes shared intermediate results. Because repeated composition creates a vast directed acyclic graph, exploration must prioritize promising nodes instead of materializing every possibility.

12554.sourceSearchName: feature transformation function feature transformation function
12554.title: Feature Transformation Function
12554.heading: Document

12555.sourceSearchName: feature transformation function feature transformation function
12555.title: Feature Transformation Function
12555.heading: Feature Transformation Function
12555.content:
A feature transformation function maps one or more existing variables to a derived variable. Unary functions operate on one input, binary functions combine two inputs, and compositions create deeper transformations.

The available functions form the grammar of automated feature construction. Type compatibility and semantic constraints prevent meaningless candidates, while composition depth controls expressiveness and search growth.

12556.sourceSearchName: feature transformation function feature transformation function
12556.title: Feature Transformation Function

12558.title: Feature Toggle
12558.heading: Feature Toggle
12558.content:
A feature toggle separates deployment from exposure by allowing code already present in a live build to be enabled or disabled through configuration. Teams can integrate incomplete or experimental work without making it available to every player.

Toggles support staged testing and rapid rollback, but each one adds state and maintenance cost. Temporary toggles should be removed after their decision has been made.

12561.title: Feature Team
12561.heading: Feature Team
12561.content:
A feature team is a cross-discipline group able to deliver a player-facing feature across the components and crafts it requires. Its backlog and Sprint Goals are organized around integrated value instead of one technical layer.

Feature teams reduce handoffs and support [[Whole Game Focus]], but they require shared architecture, standards, and access to specialized knowledge to avoid duplicating or diverging foundational work.

12563.sourceSearchName: feature subset selection feature subset selection
12563.title: Feature Subset Selection
12563.heading: Document

12564.sourceSearchName: feature subset selection feature subset selection
12564.title: Feature Subset Selection
12564.heading: Feature Subset Selection
12564.content:
Feature subset selection returns a chosen set of original variables judged useful for the analytical task. It differs from [[Feature Ranking]], which orders variables but does not by itself define the final subset.

Searching all possible subsets becomes exponential as dimensionality grows. Practical methods therefore use heuristics, model structure, or distributed computation while accepting that the globally best combination may remain unknown.

12567.sourceSearchName: feature standardization for clustering feature standardization for clustering
12567.title: Feature Standardization for Clustering
12567.heading: Feature Standardization for Clustering
12567.content:
Feature standardization transforms numerical attributes to comparable scales before proximity is computed. Without it, a variable measured in large units can dominate Euclidean or squared-error methods regardless of its substantive importance.

Standardization improves scale comparability but does not make all attributes equally meaningful. Its transformation should match the intended interpretation.

12570.title: Feature Selection
12570.heading: Feature Selection
12570.content:
Feature selection chooses a subset of observed variables for a prediction model. Removing weak or redundant inputs can reduce computation, improve interpretability, and prevent noise from obscuring useful relationships.

Selection retains original features, whereas feature extraction constructs new representations such as principal components. The appropriate method depends on feature dependence, data scale, and the prediction goal.

The book begins feature selection with role-based exclusions: identifiers, outputs, unusable missing fields, constants, high-cardinality fields, and predictors unavailable at scoring time. Algorithmic rankings are then interpreted within those data-quality and leakage constraints.

Feature selection can also make an otherwise infeasible analysis tractable by reducing a large candidate pool. Its value includes faster learning, improved accuracy when irrelevant information is removed, and greater model comprehensibility, although finding a globally optimal subset is generally computationally difficult.

At Big Data scale, the exponential subset space, distributed storage, streaming input, and demand for interpretability change which methods are practical. Scalable selection must balance relevance, redundancy, stability, computation, and communication rather than optimize predictive score alone.

12573.title: Feature Ranking
12573.heading: Feature Ranking
12573.content:
Feature ranking orders variables according to a relevance score or other selection criterion. Some rankers also report a weight that indicates the strength assigned by the internal metric.

A ranking is not automatically a subset because a cutoff still must be chosen and individually strong variables may be redundant together. It is useful when users need a transparent order or when exhaustive subset search is infeasible.

12575.title: Feature Lock
12575.heading: Document
12575.content:
2026-09-18 16:43

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Game Design Process and Roles]]

12576.title: Feature Lock
12576.heading: Feature Lock
12576.content:
Feature lock is the point after which no new game features may be introduced. The remaining schedule is reserved for completing, debugging, testing, balancing, and polishing the agreed design.

The transition is often driven by the time required to finish reliably rather than by a proof that the design is perfect. Adding scope after feature lock threatens both quality and release timing.

12579.title: Feature Generation
12579.heading: Feature Generation
12579.content:
Feature generation creates new variables that describe data in ways not already present in the original feature set. Image descriptors, mined sequence patterns, graph neighborhoods, and domain-specific measurements are examples.

Generation may be manual, automated, or learned. Because a large candidate pool can increase computation and overfitting, it is commonly paired with [[Feature Selection]] or an objective that favors compact, relevant representations.

12582.title: Feature Board
12582.heading: Feature Board
12582.content:
A feature board visualizes the state of complete features across the disciplines working on them. Rows distinguish features that are active or waiting, columns show the kind of work underway, and priority remains visible as cards move toward done.

Unlike a task-centered board, it exposes whether code, art, animation, design, or testing is stalling playable value. It encourages swarming, limits parallel features, and creates time for integrated tuning before a Sprint ends.

12584.sourceSearchName: feature area team feature area team
12584.title: Feature Area Team
12584.heading: Document

12585.sourceSearchName: feature area team feature area team
12585.title: Feature Area Team
12585.heading: Feature Area Team
12585.content:
A feature area team coordinates several teams working within a broad area of the game. The grouping gives related work a coherent product goal and Product Ownership layer while preserving small delivery teams beneath it.

Feature areas should follow meaningful product boundaries and evolve as the game changes. Permanent silos can reproduce separate games inside one release.

12586.sourceSearchName: feature area team feature area team
12586.title: Feature Area Team
12586.heading: References

12588.title: Feature Engineering
12588.heading: Feature Engineering
12588.content:
Feature engineering changes how data objects are represented so an analytic method can use their relevant structure. It includes feature transformation, generation, extraction, selection, analysis, evaluation, automated construction, and application-specific design.

Its purpose is not simply to increase the number of variables. The engineered representation should improve the task at hand while remaining computationally manageable and, when needed, understandable. Different data types and applications therefore demand different construction and selection strategies.

12591.title: Feature Descriptor
12591.heading: Feature Descriptor
12591.content:
A feature descriptor encodes the local image appearance around an interest point into a form that can be compared efficiently. A useful descriptor remains distinctive while tolerating expected changes in scale, rotation, illumination, or viewpoint.

Descriptors from the current camera image are searched against descriptors in a tracking model. A close descriptor match proposes a point correspondence, which geometry must then verify before it influences pose.

12593.sourceSearchName: feathering a composite edge feathering a composite edge
12593.title: Feathering a Composite Edge
12593.heading: Document

12594.sourceSearchName: feathering a composite edge feathering a composite edge
12594.title: Feathering a Composite Edge
12594.heading: Feathering a Composite Edge
12594.content: A hard-edged matte can reveal where two photographed plates meet. Feathering or alpha blur turns that abrupt boundary into a gradual mixture and can hide minor differences in the edge position. The book's sky-augmentation example begins with a large rectangular mask that visibly cuts across the sky; a modest edge feather makes the join less conspicuous. Feathering does not repair wrong light direction, color, or perspective, so those cues must also be checked. See [[Sky Augmentation versus Extraction]].

12595.sourceSearchName: feathering a composite edge feathering a composite edge
12595.title: Feathering a Composite Edge
12595.heading: References

12597.title: Feasible Solution
12597.heading: Feasible Solution
12597.content:
A feasible solution satisfies every constraint and sign restriction of an optimization problem. The collection of all such points is the feasible region.

Feasibility is separate from quality: a feasible point need not be an [[Optimal Solution]]. If no point satisfies all constraints, the model is infeasible.

12599.title: FBX Game Asset Export
12599.heading: Document

12600.sourceSearchName: fbx game asset export fbx game asset export
12600.title: FBX Game Asset Export
12600.heading: FBX Game Asset Export
12600.content:
FBX can export meshes, curves, empties, cameras, lights, armatures, and animation-related data through one widely supported asset container. Blender's options also select active collections or selected objects and apply coordinate and scale conversion.

Geometry settings control smoothing, loose edges, tangent space, and subdivision handling, while armature settings control bone axes and deform-only filtering. A game pipeline should save a tested preset because broad format support does not guarantee identical defaults across tools.

12603.sourceSearchName: faraday s law faraday s law
12603.title: Faraday's Law
12603.heading: Faraday's Law
12603.content:
Faraday's law states that an induced electromotive force equals the negative rate of change of magnetic flux linkage:

$$\mathcal{E}=-\frac{d(N\Phi)}{dt}.$$

Flux can change through field strength, area, orientation, or relative motion. Faster change or more turns produces a larger induced emf.

12606.sourceSearchName: faraday magnetohydrodynamic generator faraday magnetohydrodynamic generator
12606.title: Faraday Magnetohydrodynamic Generator
12606.heading: Faraday Magnetohydrodynamic Generator
12606.content: A Faraday [[Magnetohydrodynamic Generator]] extracts current across the duct in the direction perpendicular to both fluid flow and magnetic field. Electrodes on opposing walls collect the induced current as the conducting fluid crosses field lines. It differs from the Hall arrangement, which draws current along the flow direction. The electrode geometry is therefore part of how induced electrical power is collected.

12609.title: Far-Field Speech Recognition
12609.heading: Far-Field Speech Recognition
12609.content:
Far-field speech recognition handles speech captured at a distance from the microphone. The signal is weakened and mixed with room reverberation, background noise, and voices or sounds from other directions.

Microphone arrays and [[Beamforming]] can improve the target signal, but distance remains a major source of [[Acoustic Variability]] for home assistants and social robots.

12612.sourceSearchName: family wise error rate family wise error rate
12612.title: Family-Wise Error Rate
12612.heading: Family-Wise Error Rate
12612.content:
The family-wise error rate is the probability that a collection of hypothesis tests produces at least one [[False Positive]]. It treats any erroneous rejection within the family as an error event.

Controlling this probability is appropriate when even one false claim is costly, but it can be overly strict for discovery studies that expect to validate a candidate list later. The [[Bonferroni Correction]] provides a general conservative control.

12615.title: False Positive
12615.heading: False Positive
12615.content:
A false positive occurs when a procedure declares a feature significant even though its null hypothesis is true. It is a type I error at the level of an individual decision.

When thousands of features are tested, several false positives can occur in one experiment. Multiple-testing procedures therefore summarize or control how these errors accumulate across the entire selected set.

12618.sourceSearchName: false discovery rate false discovery rate
12618.title: False Discovery Rate
12618.heading: False Discovery Rate
12618.content:
The false discovery rate is the expected [[False Discovery Proportion]] across repeated experiments. It controls the average share of erroneous findings among the features selected rather than the probability of making any error at all.

This criterion is less stringent than [[Family-Wise Error Rate]] control and can yield a useful candidate list in discovery-oriented studies. The tolerated rate must still match the cost and validation plan of the scientific application.

12620.heading: Document

12621.title: False Negative
12621.heading: False Negative
12621.content:
A false negative occurs when a procedure fails to select a feature whose alternative hypothesis is true. It is a type II error and represents a missed signal rather than a spurious discovery.

Stricter thresholds can reduce [[False Positive|false positives]] while increasing false negatives. Useful high-throughput procedures therefore balance specificity against sensitivity instead of minimizing one error type without regard to the other.

12623.title: False Discovery Proportion

12624.sourceSearchName: false discovery proportion false discovery proportion
12624.title: False Discovery Proportion
12624.heading: False Discovery Proportion
12624.content:
The false discovery proportion is the number of [[False Positive|false positives]] divided by the total number of features selected by a procedure. It is defined as zero when no features are selected.

Because both the selected list and its mistaken members change across repeated datasets, the proportion is a random variable. Its expected value gives the [[False Discovery Rate]].

12627.heading: Faithfully Flat Module
12627.content:
A faithfully flat module is flat and also detects nonzero modules or failures of exactness after tensoring. Tensoring with it preserves and reflects the relevant algebraic information.

Faithful flatness lets properties such as regular sequences be checked after scalar extension. It is stronger than ordinary [[Flat Module|flatness]], which preserves exactness without necessarily detecting whether an object vanished.

12630.title: False Alarm Model
12630.heading: False Alarm Model
12630.content:
A false alarm model represents the possibility that a sensor reports a detection even though the target or event is absent. A Boolean hidden variable can select between the ordinary sensor distribution and a false-alarm distribution.

Inference then considers both explanations instead of forcing every positive reading to be caused by the searched state. The prior probability and observation pattern determine how much support is assigned to the false-alarm branch.

12633.sourceSearchName: fairness through unawareness fairness through unawareness
12633.title: Fairness Through Unawareness
12633.heading: Fairness Through Unawareness
12633.content:
Fairness through unawareness is the strategy of withholding a protected characteristic from an algorithm so the system cannot explicitly use it. The approach aims to make the decision formally blind to traits such as race or gender.

Unawareness is insufficient when other variables act as proxies or when historical outcomes already reflect unequal conditions. It can also prevent measurement of whether results disadvantage a protected group. Fairness may require knowledge of group effects and, in some cases, corrective action. The strategy therefore addresses direct discrimination but not the full problem of [[Algorithmic Bias]].

12634.title: Fairness Through Unawareness
12634.heading: References

12636.title: Faithful Module
12636.heading: Faithful Module
12636.content:
A faithful module is a module whose [[Module Annihilator]] is zero. No nonzero scalar acts as zero on every module element.

Any module M becomes faithful when regarded over the quotient R/Ann(M). Faithfulness therefore separates properties of the module action from ring elements that the action cannot detect.

12638.title: Failure as Design Evidence
12638.heading: Document

12639.sourceSearchName: failure as design evidence failure as design evidence
12639.title: Failure as Design Evidence
12639.heading: Failure as Design Evidence
12639.content:
A failed prototype is productive when it reveals that an assumption about action, comprehension, technology, or experience was wrong. Discovering that mismatch early gives the team information while the design is still cheap to change.

The useful response is neither to hide the failure nor to treat it as proof that the entire idea is worthless. The team identifies what the result teaches, revises the question, and runs another cycle.

12642.sourceSearchName: fail safe defaults fail safe defaults
12642.title: Fail-Safe Defaults
12642.heading: Fail-Safe Defaults
12642.content:
Fail-safe defaults deny access unless permission has been explicitly granted. When a decision or component fails, the system remains in a protected state instead of silently allowing an operation.

The principle reverses the burden of proof: authorization must be demonstrated. It is especially important when configurations are incomplete, errors occur, or new resources appear before policies are updated.

12645.title: Factory Method Pattern
12645.heading: Factory Method Pattern
12645.content: A factory method centralizes the decision about which concrete implementation to create and returns it through a shared type. The inventory application's command factory maps textual input such as add, get, update, or quit to a corresponding command object, so the command loop need not contain each constructor and its dependencies. A new command changes the creation boundary rather than every caller that executes commands.

12647.title: Factorization by Inspection
12647.heading: Document

12648.sourceSearchName: factorization by inspection factorization by inspection
12648.title: Factorization by Inspection
12648.heading: Factorization by Inspection
12648.content:
Factorization by inspection searches possible factor pairs and tests which product reproduces a polynomial's coefficients. For a quadratic trinomial, signs and the factors of the leading and constant coefficients constrain the possible binomials.

Inspection is systematic trial rather than unsupported guessing. Each candidate is checked through [[Polynomial Expansion]], and symmetry can reduce the cases. It works efficiently when coefficients are small and integer factors exist. A quadratic that does not factor conveniently over integers may require [[Completing the Square]] or the [[Quadratic Formula]].

12649.sourceSearchName: factorization by inspection factorization by inspection
12649.title: Factorization by Inspection
12649.heading: References

12650.sourceSearchName: factoring by grouping factoring by grouping
12650.title: Factoring by Grouping
12650.heading: Document

12651.sourceSearchName: factoring by grouping factoring by grouping
12651.title: Factoring by Grouping
12651.heading: Factoring by Grouping
12651.content:
Factoring by grouping partitions a polynomial into smaller groups, factors each group, and looks for a repeated expression. For example,

$$ax^2+a+bx^2+b=a(x^2+1)+b(x^2+1)=(a+b)(x^2+1).$$

The first grouping may require terms to be rearranged through the [[Commutative Property]]. Success depends on producing the same factor from each group. Once that repeated expression appears, the [[Distributive Property]] is used backward again to complete the factorization.

12652.title: Factoring by Grouping
12652.heading: References

12654.title: Factoring Out a Common Factor
12654.heading: Factoring Out a Common Factor
12654.content:
Factoring out a common factor uses the [[Distributive Property]] backward. If every term contains (g), then

$$ga+gb+gc=g(a+b+c).$$

The usual choice is the [[Greatest Common Factor of Terms]], which leaves the simplest integer coefficients and lowest remaining exponents. A negative common factor can be useful when it makes the leading term inside parentheses positive. Expansion provides an immediate check that no term or sign was lost.

12657.title: Factorial Time Complexity
12657.heading: Factorial Time Complexity
12657.content:
Factorial time complexity, written $O(n!)$, grows according to the product of every positive integer through $n$. It often appears when an algorithm enumerates every possible ordering or route.

The growth is even faster than [[Exponential Time Complexity]]. A brute-force solution to the [[Traveling Salesman Problem]] can examine all tours, making even a few dozen cities beyond the reach of straightforward exhaustive search.

12660.title: Factor Theorem
12660.heading: Factor Theorem
12660.content:
The factor theorem states that c is a root of a polynomial a(x) over a field exactly when x-c divides a(x). It follows by applying the polynomial division algorithm with divisor x-c.

Repeated use extracts known roots as linear factors.

12663.title: Factorable Quadratic
12663.heading: Factorable Quadratic
12663.content:
A factorable quadratic is a quadratic polynomial that can be expressed as a product of lower-degree factors over the number system being used. For example,

$$x^2+5x+6=(x+2)(x+3)$$

over the integers.

Factorability depends on the allowed coefficients. The polynomial (x^2-2) has no factorization into integer-coefficient linear factors, although it factors using irrational coefficients. When convenient factors are unavailable, a quadratic equation can still be solved through [[Completing the Square]] or the [[Quadratic Formula]].

12666.title: Factor
12666.heading: Factor
12666.content:
A factor is a number or expression multiplied with another to produce a product. In

$$12x^2=3x\cdot4x,$$

(3x) and (4x) are factors of (12x^2). A factor must divide the product exactly within the number or expression system being used.

Recognizing factors permits cancellation in fractions and supports [[Polynomial Factorization]]. A common factor divides every term of a sum and can be taken outside parentheses through the [[Distributive Property]]. Terms joined by addition are not themselves cancellable factors until the expression is factored.

12668.title: Factor Space Metric Shortcut

12669.sourceSearchName: factor space metric shortcut factor space metric shortcut
12669.title: Factor Space Metric Shortcut
12669.heading: Factor Space Metric Shortcut
12669.content:
The complete correspondence-analysis factor map preserves chi-squared distances among source profiles as Euclidean distances. When a task requires only a particular distance to an average profile, the book shows that it can be calculated directly from the original counts and marginals without computing every factor.

For massive data this can avoid a costly full eigenreduction while retaining the specified metric quantity. It does not provide the complete factor coordinates or every interpretation available from the full map; the shortcut is useful only when the requested measure is one of the identities preserved by that map.

The mapping should preserve an audit trail and avoid collapsing distinctions that matter to the analysis.

12678.heading: Factor Inertia
12678.content:
In correspondence analysis, inertia is the mass-weighted squared distance of a point cloud from its center. Eigenvalue decomposition splits that total inertia among ordered factors, so the early factors capture larger portions of the table's variation.

A two-dimensional plot is an approximation when it displays only two factors. The book repeatedly distinguishes visual interpretation from calculations in the full factor space: a low percentage of displayed inertia should make an analyst cautious about claims based solely on a planar diagram.

12681.heading: Factor Analysis
12681.content:
Factor analysis models correlations among observed variables through a smaller collection of [[Hidden Factor|hidden factors]] and feature-specific noise. Each observation is represented as a weighted combination of the common factors plus an independent residual.

The source connects factor estimation to leading principal components under suitable assumptions. For gene-expression data, the factors can summarize shared sample structure that ordinary independent-error linear models fail to represent.

12684.title: Facilitation
12684.heading: Facilitation
12684.content:
Facilitation structures a group's participation so it can explore information, make decisions, and reach workable agreement. A facilitator manages the process and access to the conversation while participants retain ownership of the content and result.

Clear purpose, visible information, balanced participation, and explicit decision rules reduce domination and premature closure. Facilitation is especially useful when expertise is distributed across disciplines.

Facial emotion recognition estimates visible expression categories from an image of a face. The service does not return a certain statement about a person's inner state; it returns model scores for categories learned from labeled examples.

The mobile application selects the highest-scoring returned category for one detected face. The book warns against anthropomorphizing the algorithm because the result depends on training examples and can be distorted by incorrectly labeled data.

Face clustering groups detected face instances by identity or visual similarity, often combining appearance with contextual evidence from images, videos, captions, or co-occurrence. Annotation assigns a name or semantic label to the resulting groups.

Pose, lighting, expression, age, and detection error create large within-person variation. Context can improve grouping but may also reinforce mistaken associations, so representative examples and uncertain assignments should be reviewed.

12705.title: F-Measure for Classification
12705.heading: F-Measure for Classification
12705.content:
The F-measure for classification is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. The F1 score weights them equally, while the more general F-beta score places greater emphasis on recall when beta is above one and on precision when it is below one.

Because both components depend on the chosen positive class and decision threshold, the score should be interpreted with the application's error costs and class distribution in view.

The book calculates the measure from held-out confusion-matrix counts so a model must balance successful positive retrieval against the reliability of positive predictions. The appropriate balance remains dependent on the costs of false positives and false negatives.

12708.title: F-Distribution
12708.heading: F-Distribution
12708.content:
The F-distribution is a positive, right-skewed probability family parameterized by two degrees of freedom. It arises from ratios of scaled variance estimates and supplies the reference distribution for many analysis-of-variance statistics.

The source also uses a scaled F model for gene-specific sample variances in an empirical Bayes hierarchy. This permits a shared distribution to stabilize many noisy variance estimates.

Tags: [[Adaptive and Outcome-Based Cyber Defense]]

12711.title: Extrusion Detection
12711.heading: Extrusion Detection
12711.content:
Extrusion detection monitors information and communication leaving a protected environment. It reverses the usual emphasis on stopping entry by looking for data theft, unexpected command traffic, or other evidence that an internal system is already compromised.

Outbound destinations, volumes, timing, and content patterns can reveal [[Cyber Command and Control]] or collection by [[Spyware]]. The approach supports [[Outcome-Based Cyber Defense]] by concentrating on the attempted loss of information.

12714.title: Extrinsic Semiconductor
12714.heading: Extrinsic Semiconductor
12714.content: An extrinsic semiconductor has controlled impurities that add allowed levels within the [[Semiconductor Band Gap]]. Donor impurities provide electrons near the conduction band, producing [[N-Type Semiconductor]] material. Acceptor impurities create electron deficiencies near the valence band, producing [[P-Type Semiconductor]] material. This is the electronic result of [[Semiconductor Doping]], not a different base crystal.

12717.title: Extreme Programming
12717.heading: Extreme Programming
12717.content:
Extreme Programming is a set of engineering practices for sustaining rapid change through technical feedback and collaboration. Practices include [[Test-Driven Development]], [[Continuous Integration]], [[Pair Programming]], simple design, and frequent refactoring.

Scrum can organize the product and team cadence while XP strengthens the way code is created inside that cadence. The practices make small iterations safer rather than trading speed for accumulating instability.

12720.title: Extrusion Bioprinting
12720.heading: Extrusion Bioprinting
12720.content:
Extrusion bioprinting deposits a continuous filament of cell-compatible material through a nozzle and builds a three-dimensional structure layer by layer. Nozzle path, pressure, gelation, and ink rheology determine shape fidelity and cell stress.

The method can build comparatively large tissues and channels, but soft hydrogels may buckle or collapse without temporary support.

12723.title: Extreme Gradient Boosting
12723.heading: Extreme Gradient Boosting
12723.content:
Extreme gradient boosting builds an additive sequence of trees, with each new tree reducing errors left by the current ensemble. Regularization, learning rate, tree depth, and iteration count control the balance between fit and generalization.

The book applies XGBoost to a sparse encoded matrix and evaluates the resulting probabilities on held-out data.

12726.title: Extraneous Solution
12726.heading: Extraneous Solution
12726.content: An extraneous solution satisfies a transformed equation but not the original one. It can arise from a nonreversible step such as squaring both sides, multiplying by an expression that may be zero, or clearing a denominator whose zero is excluded. Substitution into the original equation is therefore part of solving radical and rational equations.

12729.heading: External-Internal Index
12729.content:
The external-internal index compares links crossing an attributed group boundary with links remaining inside the group. It subtracts internal ties from external ties and divides by their total, producing values from negative one to positive one.

Negative values indicate stronger within-group connection, while positive values indicate more outward connection. In a legislature, the grouping attribute can be party, seniority, or political position.

12732.title: Extracellular Matrix
12732.heading: Extracellular Matrix
12732.content:
Extracellular matrix is the network of proteins and other molecules surrounding cells in tissue. It provides physical support, adhesion sites, mechanical cues, and biochemical signals that influence cell survival, organization, and function.

Biofabrication uses natural matrix materials or synthetic mimics to recreate selected aspects of this environment around cultured cells.

An external stylesheet is attached to an HTML document with a `link` element whose relationship is `stylesheet`. The browser retrieves the referenced CSS resource and applies its rules to the document, allowing one file to provide shared presentation across many pages.

Media restrictions, alternate stylesheets, and resource URLs can be declared on the link. Compared with [[Embedded CSS Style Sheets]], external linking separates presentation from an individual document and makes reuse easier.

12747.title: Exterior Power
12747.heading: Exterior Power
12747.content:
The n-th exterior power ∧ⁿM is obtained from the n-fold tensor product by imposing alternating relations, so tensors with repeated factors vanish and swapping factors changes sign.

Exterior powers encode oriented multilinear combinations. The [[Koszul Complex]] of a sequence is built from exterior powers of a free module, with differentials determined by the sequence elements.

12750.title: Extension Theorem
12750.heading: Extension Theorem
12750.content:
The extension theorem gives conditions under which a partial solution of an [[Elimination Ideal]] can be extended by a value for the eliminated variable to solve the original polynomial system.

Leading coefficients of the original equations identify exceptional partial solutions where extension can fail. The theorem complements the closure result: elimination describes projected equations, while extension determines when those projected points lift to actual solutions.

12752.title: Extension Field
12752.heading: Document
12752.content:

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Field Extensions and Polynomial Roots]]

12753.title: Extension Field
12753.heading: Extension Field
12753.content:
An extension field E of K contains K as a subfield with the same addition and multiplication on elements of K. It provides a larger setting in which polynomials over K may acquire roots.

The notation K ⊆ E records both containment and compatible field structure.

12756.title: Extended Ideal
12756.heading: Extended Ideal
12756.content:
Given a [[Ring Homomorphism]] f: R → T and an [[Ideal]] I of R, the extended ideal Iᵉ is the ideal of T generated by f(I). It includes all finite T-linear combinations of images of elements of I.

Under [[Ring Localization]], extension sends I to S⁻¹I. Extending and then contracting can enlarge an ideal when elements annihilated by denominators become indistinguishable.

12759.title: Ext Functor
12759.heading: Ext Functor
12759.content:
Extⁿ_R(M,N) is a derived form of the [[Hom Module]]. It can be computed by applying Hom to a projective resolution of M or an injective resolution of N and taking cohomology.

Ext⁰ equals Hom. Positive-degree Ext records higher extension obstructions and is used by the source to characterize depth, grade, and injective dimension.

12762.title: Expressive Game System
12762.heading: Expressive Game System
12762.content:
An expressive game system communicates ideas through rules and the experiences those rules produce. Its message is carried not only by text or imagery, but by what players can do, what resists them, and what consequences follow.

Because players participate in producing the experience, the system can express relationships and feelings that are difficult to state directly. [[Story as System]] is one use of this broader expressive capacity.

12765.title: Expression Evaluation
12765.heading: Expression Evaluation
12765.content:
Expression evaluation finds the numerical value of an [[Algebraic Expression]] for specified values of its variables. The values are inserted through [[Substitution]], then operations are performed according to the expression's grouping and precedence.

For (a^3+b^3+3ab) with (a=1) and (b=2), evaluation replaces every occurrence consistently before calculating. Parentheses around substituted negative values are important because ((-2)^2) differs from (-2^2). Evaluation checks a formula at a particular assignment; it does not prove an [[Algebraic Identity]] for all assignments.

12774.title: Exponentiation
12774.heading: Exponentiation
12774.content:
Exponentiation is the operation that raises a base to a power. For a natural number (n\geq1),

$$a^n=\underbrace{a\cdot a\cdots a}_{n\text{ factors}}.$$

Here (a) is the [[Base of a Power]] and (n) is the [[Exponent]]. Exponentiation abbreviates repeated multiplication, just as multiplication abbreviates repeated addition for natural numbers. It is evaluated before multiplication and addition unless [[Grouping Symbols]] specify another structure. Its inverse operation is expressed through a [[Root]].

12780.heading: Exponential Time Complexity

Exponential time complexity has a variable in the exponent, such as $O(2^n)$. Each modest increase in [[Input Size]] can multiply the required work, causing runtime to exceed physical limits quickly.

An exponential [[Algorithm]] may prove that a solution can be found in principle without providing a practical method. When no efficient exact method is known, an [[Approximation Algorithm]] may trade guaranteed optimality for a useful answer obtainable in reasonable time.

12783.heading: Exponential Survival Distribution
12783.content:
The exponential survival distribution assumes a constant hazard rate over time. Its simplicity yields a direct parametric model, but the implied event process is restrictive for risks that rise, fall, or change with age.

An exponential fitted curve should be compared with the nonparametric survival experience. Visible departure or contradictory conclusions relative to other plausible models are reasons to reject the assumption or report substantial sensitivity.

Exponential scaling in hyperbolic space means that circumference and area grow exponentially with radius. Small neighborhoods near the center look nearly flat, while equal-area regions appear increasingly compressed near the boundary of a disk visualization.

This growth mirrors the number of nodes found at successive depths of a branching tree. The correspondence helps explain why [[Hyperbolic Space]] can represent hierarchical and scale-free networks with low dimensionality.

12789.heading: Exponent
12789.content:
An exponent is the raised value in a [[Power]] that specifies repeated multiplication or an extension of that pattern. In (a^n), (n) is the exponent and (a) is the base.

A positive integer exponent counts copies of the base. A [[Zero Exponent]] makes a nonzero base equal one, and a [[Negative Exponent]] denotes the reciprocal of a positive power. Parentheses determine what the exponent acts on: ((-a)^2) squares the negative quantity, while (-a^2) takes the opposite after squaring (a).

12792.title: Exponential Function
12792.heading: Exponential Function
12792.content: An exponential function has the form $f(x)=a^x$ for a positive base $a\ne1$. Its domain is all real numbers, its values are positive, and it passes through $(0,1)$. It grows when $a>1$ and decays when $0<a<1$. Its inverse is the logarithm with the same base.

12795.title: Exponent Laws
12795.heading: Exponent Laws
12795.content: Exponent laws summarize repeated multiplication. For a nonzero base, $a^ma^n=a^{m+n}$, $a^m/a^n=a^{m-n}$, $(a^m)^n=a^{mn}$, and $a^{-n}=1/a^n$. These rules preserve the base while changing how many factors remain, and they extend naturally to [[Scientific Notation]] and [[Rational Exponent]]s.

12798.title: Explosion Diagram
12798.heading: Explosion Diagram
12798.content:
An explosion diagram separates the components of an assembled object along controlled directions so internal structure and part relationships become visible. In AR, the diagram can remain registered with the physical assembly while virtual components move into a more legible arrangement.

The transformation must preserve correspondence between each displaced part and its original location. It is especially useful when direct transparency would create excessive visual interference.
